title: USC and UCLA Bet Big on AI to Meet Soaring Student, Job Market Demands
author: Jaweed Kaleem
summary: Kaleem reports on two California universities making opposite bets on the same technology. USC's Viterbi School is launching an undergraduate artificial intelligence degree housed in its computing and AI school, built to teach students to design and build models rather than merely use them, with a required semester-long ethics course and syllabus questions about liability for self-driving cars and bias in policing algorithms. UCLA is converting a fifteen-year-old digital humanities minor, now one of its most popular, into a department, with professors shifting appointments and funding into the major. Kaleem is careful to let the UCLA faculty define their posture as neither promotional nor condemnatory, and quotes Todd Presner on teaching students that large language models did not appear from nowhere in 2022 but rest on seven decades of statistical work on language, and on exercises where students build historical narratives with models and then manipulate them to expose the possibilities for disinformation. The piece situates both programs in a wider map: UC Santa Barbara and San Diego State launching AI majors, Carnegie Mellon, MIT and Penn already granting them, and Stanford, Berkeley and Caltech pointedly declining to create undergraduate AI degrees. Michael Horn supplies the analytic frame, reading the launches as universities meeting market demand and warning that slow academic review may leave new courses out of date, while graduates of the UCLA minor describe it as the thing recruiters asked about.
points: The two programs make opposite pitches from the same technology: USC signals that AI is more than coding, while UCLA argues the humanities matter more in an AI era.
Stanford, Berkeley and Caltech have declined to create undergraduate AI majors, treating AI as a track or a capability to be applied across fields rather than a degree.

UCLA's digital humanities courses include historical and critical approaches, tracing model lineage to statistical language work of the late 1940s and having students manipulate generated narratives to expose distortion.
Nearly all the new AI programs require ethics coursework, framed around concrete liability and bias questions rather than abstract principle.
Horn's warning about program obsolescence cuts against the market-demand rationale, since approval timelines may outlast the state of the field a course was written to teach.
quotes: USC and UCLA are joining the rush to embed artificial intelligence and new digital technologies into college coursework as the academic year begins, announcing new AI majors and initiatives, betting that degrees built partly or entirely around AI will launch careers and pay off after graduation.
Not every campus is creating a major. Neither Stanford nor UC Berkeley, the state’s two biggest computer science powers, has created an undergraduate AI degree.
They’re meeting market demand,” Horn said. Universities are getting “a signal from both students and families” that what students learn needs to be relevant, he said.

Horn said the real risk is that any new educational program now will age badly. By the time a course is written and approved through a typically slow academic review, the teaching could be “out of date or in a different direction from the field,” Horn said.

According to the course syllabus, students examine questions such as: Who is responsible when a self-driving car injures someone or damages property? How does bias enter algorithms used in policing? What is the hidden human labor behind tech systems advertised as automated?

Murali Annavaram, a professor of electrical and computer engineering, likened AI to a calculator. It frees a student from memorizing all formulas, such as pi to the fourth decimal, but not from knowing whether an answer is right, he said.

We didn’t just get large language models in 2022 out of nowhere,” he said. “There was about seven decades of work that had to happen,” he said, tracing the origins to the late 1940s and early 1950s and studies on the statistics of language.
Kurtz said the aim is to prepare students “not just to navigate and use technology ethically, but to critically shape it as they move into the workforce.
